title: Model Fusion via Retrofitting
claim: Fusion can be done by clustering neurons of parent models into centroids and training the fused layer to match them, level by level.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right; dashed colored arrows converge on centroid dots
description: A single wide diagram showing small fully connected MLPs drawn as gray node-and-edge graphs. At left, Model 1 and Model 2 are stacked vertically. A thick black arrow labeled 'Compute activations and group neurons' leads to copies of both models in the middle, where hidden neurons of the first layer are colored red, green, blue and yellow to mark cluster membership. Dashed red and blue curved arrows run from the matching neurons in both models to four colored centroid dots at the top right, labeled 'centroids'. At bottom right, the Fused model F has its first hidden layer circled in magenta. A black arrow from the circle points to the centroids, with the text 'Fit weights to minimize distance between fused activations and centroids'. The eye goes first to the colorful dashed arrows converging on the centroids.
caption: Overview of our method. Given two MLPs with two hidden layers of size 4, we compute the layer activations, cluster their neurons, and train the first layer of the fused model to match the centroids with the MSE loss. The process is repeated in subsequent levels.
abstract: Model fusion seeks to combine independently trained neural networks into a single model without retraining, but is complicated by representational divergence arising from permutation invariance, random initialization, and heterogeneous training data. Existing methods struggle particularly in zero-shot settings under non-IID data distributions, and are often limited to specific architectures or pairwise fusion. We introduce a neuron-centric family of fusion algorithms that frames fusion as a principled representation-matching problem: intermediate neurons across parent models are grouped into target representations, which the fused model's corresponding sub-networks are then trained to approximate. Unlike prior work, our approach incorporates neuron attribution scores to bias alignment toward salient features, and can be applied to any architecture modularizable as a DAG of levels -- empirically validated on VGGs, ResNets, and ViTs. Experiments across standard benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing fusion methods, with the largest gains in zero-shot and non-IID scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/AndrewSpano/model-fusion-via-retrofitting.
